The '''Allen Telescope Array''' ('''ATA'''), formerly known as the '''One Hectare Telescope''' ('''1hT'''), is a [[radio telescope]] [[astronomical interferometer|array]] dedicated to astronomical observations and a simultaneous [[search for extraterrestrial intelligence]] (SETI).<ref>{{cite news | first=Daniel | last=Terdiman | author-link=Daniel Terdiman | url=https://www.cnet.com/culture/setis-large-scale-telescope-scans-the-skies/ | title=SETI's large-scale telescope scans the skies | date=12 December 2008 | work=CNET News | access-date=2008-12-12 | archive-date=2014-02-01 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201143419/http://news.cnet.com/8301-13772_3-10121889-52.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=John Johnson Jr. |url=http://www.latimes.com/news/printedition/front/la-sci-seti1-2008jun01,0,1621324.story |title=Aliens get a new switchboard: a SETI radio telescope in Northern California |date=1 June 2008 |work=The Los Angeles Times |access-date=2008-09-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004224517/http://www.latimes.com/news/printedition/front/la-sci-seti1-2008jun01%2C0%2C1621324.story |archive-date=4 October 2008 }}</ref> The array is situated at the [[Hat Creek Radio Observatory]] in [[Shasta County, California|Shasta County]], {{convert|290|mi}} northeast of [[San Francisco]], California.

The project was originally developed as a joint effort between the [[SETI Institute]] and the [[Radio Astronomy Laboratory]] (RAL) at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (UC Berkeley), with funds obtained from an initial {{US$|link=yes}}12.5 million donation by the [[Paul G. Allen Family Foundation]] and [[Nathan Myhrvold]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Microsoft moguls back search for ET intelligence |journal=Nature |date=1 August 2000 |volume=406 |issue=6796 |page=551 |doi=10.1038/35020722 |language=en |issn=1476-4687|last1=Dalton |first1=Rex |pmid=10949267 |s2cid=4415108 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  The first phase of construction was completed and the ATA finally became operational on 11 October 2007 with 42 antennas (ATA-42), after [[Paul Allen]] (co-founder of [[Microsoft]]) had pledged an additional $13.5 million to support the construction of the first and second phases.<ref name="NYT10-07">{{cite news | author=Dennis Overbye | title=Stretching the Search for Signs of Life | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/11/science/11seti.html | work=The New York Times | date=11 October 2007 | access-date=2009-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | author=Staff writers | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/technology/7041183.stm | title=Skies to be swept for alien life | date=12 October 2007 | work=BBC News | access-date=2007-10-12 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071012223754/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/technology/7041183.stm| archive-date= 12 October 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref>

Although overall Allen has contributed more than $30 million to the project, it has not succeeded in building the 350 6.1&nbsp;m (20&nbsp;ft) dishes originally conceived,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://archive.seti.org/pdfs/Shostak-spring2009-EnS.pdf |title=When Will We Find the Extraterrestrials? |last1=Shostak |first1=Seth |date=2009 |website=SETI.org |publisher=Engineering & Science |access-date=20 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150415115307/http://archive.seti.org/pdfs/Shostak-spring2009-EnS.pdf |archive-date=15 April 2015 }}</ref> and the project The facility is now managed by [[SRI International]] (formerly Stanford Research Institute), an independent, nonprofit research institute.<ref>{{cite web | author=Robert Sanders | title=UC Berkeley passes management of Allen Telescope Array to SRI | url=http://newscenter.berkeley.edu/2012/04/13/uc-berkeley-passes-management-of-allen-telescope-array-to-sri/ | publisher=UC Berkeley NewsCenter | date=April 13, 2012 | access-date=29 December 2012 | archive-date=23 October 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023061917/http://newscenter.berkeley.edu/2012/04/13/uc-berkeley-passes-management-of-allen-telescope-array-to-sri/ }}</ref> As of 2016, the [[SETI Institute]] performs observations<ref>{{cite web | last = Harp | first = Gerald R. | author-link = Gerald R. Harp | title = SETI Signal Searching | website = SETI.org | publisher = [[SETI Institute]] | url = http://setiquest.info/index.html | access-date = 7 July 2016 | archive-date = 5 June 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190605174204/http://setiquest.info/index.html }}</ref>  with the ATA between the hours of 6 pm and 6 am daily.

In August 2014, the installation was threatened by a forest fire in the area and was briefly forced to shut down, but ultimately emerged largely unscathed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.seti.org/node/2197 |title=Forest Fires in Vicinity of Allen Telescope Array |last1=Shostak |first1=Seth |date=8 August 2014 |website=SETI.org |publisher=SETI Institute |access-date=20 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221045622/http://www.seti.org/node/2197 |archive-date=21 February 2015 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

==Overview==
First conceived by [[SETI]] pioneer [[Frank Drake]], the idea has been a dream of the [[SETI Institute]] for years. However, it was not until early 2001 that research and development began, after a donation of $11.5 million by the [[Paul G. Allen Family Foundation]]. In March 2004, following the successful completion of a three-year research and development phase, the SETI Institute unveiled a three-tier construction plan for the telescope. Construction began immediately, thanks to the pledge of $13.5 million by [[Paul Allen]] (co-founder of [[Microsoft]]) to support the construction of the first and second phases. The SETI Institute named the telescope in Allen's honor. Overall, Paul Allen  contributed more than $30 million to the project.

The ATA is a centimeter-wave [[Astronomical interferometer|array]] which pioneers the Large-Number Small-Diameter concept of building [[radio telescope]]s. Compared to a large [[dish antenna]], large numbers of smaller dishes are cheaper for the same collecting area. To get similar sensitivity, the signals from all telescopes must be combined. This requires high-performance electronics, which had been prohibitively expensive. Due to the declining cost of electronic components, the required electronics became practicable, resulting in a large cost-saving over telescopes of more conventional design. This is informally referred to as "replacing steel with silicon".

The ATA has four primary technical capabilities that make it well suited for a range of scientific investigations: a very wide [[field of view#Astronomy|field of view]] (2.45° at λ = 21&nbsp;cm, the wavelength of the [[hydrogen line]]), complete instantaneous frequency coverage from 0.5 to 11.2&nbsp;[[gigahertz]] (GHz), multiple simultaneous backends, and active interference mitigation. The area of sky which can be instantaneously imaged is 17 times that obtainable by the [[Very Large Array]] telescope. The instantaneous frequency coverage of more than four [[Octave (electronics)|octaves]] is unprecedented in radio astronomy, and is the result of a unique feed, input amplifier and signal path design. Active interference mitigation will make it possible to observe even at the frequencies of many terrestrial [[Radio|radio emitters]].
 
All-sky surveys are an important part of the science program,{{clarify|date=March 2016}} and the ATA will have increased efficiency through its ability to conduct [[SETI|extraterrestrial intelligence searches]] (SETI) and other [[radio astronomy]] observations simultaneously. The telescope can do this by splitting the recorded signals in the control room prior to final processing. Simultaneous observations are possible because for [[SETI]], wherever the telescope is pointed, several target stars will lie within the large field of view afforded by the 6&nbsp;m dishes.  By agreement between the UC Berkeley [[Radio Astronomy Laboratory]] (RAL) and the [[SETI Institute]], the needs of conventional radio astronomy determined the pointing of the array up until 2012.

The ATA is planned to comprise 350 6 m dishes and will make possible large, deep radio surveys that were not previously feasible. The telescope design incorporates many new features, including [[Hydroforming|hydroformed]] antenna surfaces, a [[Log-periodic antenna|log-periodic]] feed covering the entire range of frequencies from 500&nbsp;[[megahertz]] (MHz) to 11.2&nbsp;GHz, and low-noise, [[Wideband|wide-band]] amplifiers with a flat response over the entire band, thus making it possible to amplify the sky signal directly. This amplified signal, containing the entire received bandwidth, is brought from each antenna to the processing room via [[optical fiber]] cables. This means that as electronics improve and wider bandwidths are obtainable, only the central processor needs to change, and not the antennas or feeds.

The instrument was operated and maintained by RAL until development of the array was put on hold in 2011. RAL worked hand in hand with the SETI Institute during design and prototyping and was the primary designer of the feed, antenna surfaces, [[beamforming]], correlator, and imaging system for radio astronomy observations.

The panel for the [[Astronomy and Astrophysics Decadal Survey]] in its fifth report, [[Astronomy and Astrophysics Decadal Survey#Astronomy and Astrophysics in the New Millennium, 2001|''Astronomy and Astrophysics in the New Millennium'']] (2001), endorsed SETI and recognized the ATA (then called the 1-[[Hectare]] Telescope) as an important stepping stone towards the building of the [[Square Kilometer Array]] telescope (SKA). The most recent Decadal report recommended ending the US's financial support of the SKA, although US participation in SKA precursors such as [[MeerKAT]], the [[Hydrogen Epoch of Reionization Array]] and the [[Murchison Widefield Array]].

Although cost estimates of unbuilt projects are always dubious, and the specifications are not identical (conventional telescopes have lower [[noise temperature]], but the ATA has a larger [[field of view#Astronomy|field of view]], for example), the ATA has potential promise as a much cheaper radio telescope technology for a given effective aperture. For example, the amount spent on the first ATA-42 phase, including technology development, is roughly one third of the cost of a new copy of a [[Deep Space Network]] 34 m antenna of similar collecting area.<ref>{{cite web | author=Shannon McConnell | title=Deep Space Network Adds a 34m Beam Wave Guide Antenna in Madrid, Spain | url=http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/features/madridnew.html | work=Deep Space Network Home | publisher=JPL | date=2005 | access-date=2009-04-14 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090416125351/http://deepspace.jpl.nasa.gov/dsn/features/madridnew.html | archive-date=16 April 2009 }}</ref> Similarly, the estimated total cost of building the remaining 308 dishes was estimated ({{as of|2007|October|lc=y}}) at about $41 million.<ref name="NYT10-07"/> This is about two times cheaper than the $85 million cost of the last large radio astronomy antenna built in the US, the [[Green Bank Telescope]], of similar collecting area. The contractor filed for a $29 million overrun, but only $4 million of this was allowed.<ref>{{cite report | author=Senior Review Committee | title=From the Ground UP: Balancing the NSF Astronomy Program | page=4.4.2.3 | publisher=National Science Foundation Division of Astronomical Sciences | url=https://www.nsf.gov/mps/ast/seniorreview/sr_report_mpsac_updated_12-1-06.pdf | date=22 October 2006 | access-date=2009-04-14| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090418132223/https://www.nsf.gov/mps/ast/seniorreview/sr_report_mpsac_updated_12-1-06.pdf | archive-date= 18 April 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>

The ATA aspires to be among the world's largest and fastest observing instruments, and to permit astronomers to search many different target stars simultaneously. If completed as originally envisioned, it will be one of the largest and most powerful telescopes in the world.

== History ==
Since its inception, the ATA has been a development tool{{clarify|date=February 2016}} for [[astronomical interferometer]] technology (specifically, for the [[Square Kilometer Array]]).<ref>{{cite journal | title=The Allen Telescope Array: The first widefield, panchromatic, snapshot radio camera for radio astronomy and SETI | first1=Jack | last1=Welch |display-authors=etal | journal=Proceedings of the IEEE | volume=97 | issue=8 | date=2009-08-01 | pages=1438–1447 | doi=10.1109/jproc.2009.2017103|arxiv = 0904.0762 |bibcode = 2009IEEEP..97.1438W | s2cid=7486677 }}</ref>

The ATA was originally planned to be constructed in four stages, ATA-42, ATA-98, ATA-206 and ATA-350, each number representing the number of dishes in the array at a given time (See Table 1). The ATA is planned to comprise 350 dishes with a diameter of 6 m each.

Regular operations with 42 dishes started on 11 October 2007.<ref name="NYT10-07"/> Funding for building additional antennas is currently being sought by the [[SETI Institute]] from various sources, including the [[United States Navy]], [[Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency]] (DARPA), [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) and private donors.

Simultaneous astronomical and SETI observations are performed with two 32-input dual [[polarization (antenna)|polarization]] [[radio correlator|imaging correlators]].<ref>{{cite web | author=W.L. Urry | author2=M. Wright | author3=M. Dexter| author4=D. MacMahon | title=The ATA Correlator ATA Memo 73| page=3 | publisher=University of California, Berkeley | url=http://www.seti.org/sites/default/files/ATA-memo-series/memo73.pdf | date=16 February 2007 | access-date=2016-07-07}}</ref> Numerous articles reporting conventional radio astronomy observations have been published.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bower | first1 = Geoffrey C. | author1-link = Geoffrey C Bower |display-authors=etal | title = The Allen Telescope Array Pi GHz Sky Survey. The workhorse SETI search system [[OpenSonATA|(SETI on ATA or SonATA)]] performs fully automated SETI observations. SonATA follows up on detected signals in real time and continues to track them until 1) the signal is shown to have been generated on Earth or rarely, 2) the source sets, which triggers follow up the next day. As of 2016, more than two hundred million signals have been followed up and classified {{citation needed |date=July 2016}} using the ATA. Not one of these signals had all the characteristics expected for an ETI signal. The results of SETI Institute's observations are published in a number of papers.<ref>Results from the Allen Telescope Array: SETI Survey of the Galactic Center Region [http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009AAS...21440707B]</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=A Radio SETI Campaign for microsec-sec Periodic Signals |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=869 |page=66 |arxiv=1506.00055 | last1=Harp | first1=G. In April 2011, the ATA was put into hibernation owing to funding shortfalls, meaning that it was no longer available for use.<ref>{{cite news | author=John Matson | title=Budget crunch mothballs telescopes built to search for alien signals | url = http://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/post.cfm?id=budget-crunch-mothballs-telescopes-2011-04-24 | work=Scientific American | date=24 April 2011 | access-date=2011-04-25| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110427204032/http://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/post.cfm?id=budget-crunch-mothballs-telescopes-2011-04-24| archive-date= 27 April 2011 | url-status= live}}</ref>  Operation of the ATA resumed on 5 December 2011.<ref name="seti905" /> Efforts are now led by [[Andrew Siemion]].<ref name="seti-chair-siemion">{{ cite web |title=Andrew Siemion Named Bernard M. Oliver Chair of SETI at the SETI Institute | url=https://seti.org/press-release/andrew-siemion-named-bernard-m-oliver-chair-seti-seti-institute |date=April 9, 2018 |publisher=SETI Institute |access-date=June 5, 2018}}</ref>

===Status===
In 2012, the ATA was funded by a $3.6 million philanthropic donation by Franklin Antonio, cofounder and Chief Scientist of [[Qualcomm Incorporated]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.redding.com/news/2012/dec/06/new-hat-creek-receivers-will-let-seti-delve-into/ |title=New Hat Creek receivers will let SETI delve deeper into space |first=Damon |last=Arthur |date=December 6, 2012 |work=Record Searchlight |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140330064010/http://www.redding.com/news/2012/dec/06/new-hat-creek-receivers-will-let-seti-delve-into/ |archive-date=2014-03-30 }}</ref> This gift supports upgrades of all the receivers on the ATA dishes to have dramatically greater sensitivity (2 − 10× from 1–8&nbsp;GHz) than before and support sensitive observations over a wider frequency range, from 1–15&nbsp;GHz, when initially the radio frequency electronics went to only 11&nbsp;GHz. By July 2016, the first ten of these receivers had been installed and proven. Beginning in 2019, the SETI Institute undertook a multi-year, Franklin Antonio–funded refurbishment of the array, equipping its dishes with new wideband "Antonio" feeds (first developed in 2015) and a new digital signal-processing system to improve its sensitivity and frequency coverage.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://astrobiology.com/2019/07/major-upgrade-of-the-allen-telescope-array.html |title=Major Upgrade Of The Allen Telescope Array |work=Astrobiology |date=2019-07-08 |access-date=2026-07-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Sheikh |first=Sofia Z. |display-authors=etal |title=The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |year=2023 |arxiv=2312.07756}}</ref> After Antonio's death in 2022, the SETI Institute announced in November 2023 that it had received a $200 million bequest from his estate—nearly ten times its annual budget—to permanently endow its core research programs.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theregister.com/offbeat/2023/11/09/late-qualcomm-cofounder-leaves-200m-to-fund-seti-research/ |title=Late Qualcomm cofounder leaves $200M to fund SETI research |work=The Register |date=2023-11-09 |access-date=2026-07-14}}</ref>

In November 2015, the ATA studied the anomalous star [[KIC 8462852]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.seti.org/seti-institute/ata-checks-out-star-kic8462852 |title=Allen Telescope Array Checks Out Star KIC 8462852 |work=SETI Institute |access-date=2016-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404161029/http://www.seti.org/seti-institute/ata-checks-out-star-kic8462852 |archive-date=2016-04-04 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=Radio SETI Observations of the Anomalous Star KIC 8462852 | last1=Harp | first1=G. R. |last2= Richards | first2=Jon| last3=Shostak| first3=Seth | last4=Tarter |first4=Jill C. | last5=Vakoch |first5=Douglas A.| last6=Munson | first6=Chris| journal=Astrophysical Journal |doi=10.3847/0004-637X/825/2/155|arxiv=1511.01606 | volume=825 | issue=2 | page=155|bibcode = 2016ApJ...825..155H | year=2016 | s2cid=102491516 | doi-access=free }}</ref> and in autumn 2017 the Allen Telescope Array examined the interstellar asteroid  [[ʻOumuamua]] for signs of technology, but detected no unusual radio emissions.<ref name=SETI>{{cite news |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/alien-probe-or-galactic-driftwood-seti-tunes-in-to-oumuamua/ |title=Alien Probe or Galactic Driftwood? SETI Tunes In to {{okina}}Oumuamua |work=Scientific American |first=Lee |last=Billings |date=11 December 2017 |access-date=2017-12-12|quote=So far limited observations of {{okina}}Oumuamua, using facilities such as the SETI Institute's Allen Telescope Array, have turned up nothing.}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2017/12/yuri-milner-oumuamua-interstellar-asteroid/547985/ |title=Astronomers to Check Mysterious Interstellar Object for Signs of Technology |magazine=The Atlantic |first=Marina |last=Koren |date=11 December 2017}}</ref>

== Key science goals ==
{{unreferenced section|date=February 2022}}
The science goals listed below represent the most important projects to be conducted with the ATA. Each of these goals is associated with one of the four stages of development mentioned earlier. (See Table 1). Also listed is some of the science that it is hoped each will produce.

* Determine the [[hydrogen line]] (HI) content of [[galaxies]] out to ''z'' ~ 0.2 over 3π [[steradian]]s, in order to measure how much [[Intergalactic space|intergalactic gas]] external galaxies are accreting; to search for dark, starless galaxies; to lay the foundation for [[dark energy]] detection by the [[Square Kilometer Array]].
* Classify 250,000 extra-galactic radio sources as [[active galactic nuclei]] or [[starburst galaxies]], in order to probe and quantify star formation in the [[Local Universe]]; to identify high [[redshift]] objects; to probe large-scale structure in the Universe; to identify gravitational lens candidates for [[dark matter]] and [[dark energy]] detection.
* Explore the [[Transient astronomical event|transient sky]], in order to probe accretion onto [[black hole]]s; to find orphan [[gamma ray burst]] afterglows; to discover new and unknown transient phenomena.
* Survey 1,000,000 stars for [[SETI]]-related emission with enough sensitivity to detect an [[Arecibo Observatory|Arecibo]] [[Radar astronomy|radar]] out to 300 [[parsec]]s within the range of 1–10&nbsp;[[GHz]].
* Survey the 4×10<sup>10</sup> stars of the inner [[Galactic coordinate system|galactic plane]] from 1.42–1.72&nbsp;GHz for very powerful [[SETI|transmitters]].
* Measure the [[magnetic field]]s in the [[Milky Way]] and other [[Local Group]] galaxies, in order to probe the role of magnetic fields in star formation and [[galaxy formation and evolution]].
* Detect the [[gravitational wave]] background from massive [[black holes]] through [[pulsar]] timing.
* Measure [[molecular cloud]] and [[star formation]] properties using new molecular tracers, in order to map star formation conditions on the scale of entire [[giant molecular clouds]] (GMCs); to determine the [[metallicity]] gradient of the Milky Way.

== Opportunistic science ==
Since construction of the [[Astronomical interferometer|array]] began, a few science goals not specifically drawn up for it have been suggested.

For example, the Allen Telescope Array has offered to provide the mooncast data downlink for any contestants in the [[Google Lunar X Prize]].<ref>{{cite press release | title=Google Sponsors Lunar X PRIZE to Create a Space Race for a New Generation | url=http://www.googlelunarxprize.org/lunar/press-release/google-sponsors-lunar-x-prize-to-create-a-space-race-for-a-new-generation | publisher=X PRIZE Foundation and Google Inc. | date=13 September 2007 | access-date=2009-04-14| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090511030914/http://www.googlelunarxprize.org/lunar/press-release/google-sponsors-lunar-x-prize-to-create-a-space-race-for-a-new-generation| archive-date= 11 May 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref> This is practical, since the array, with no modifications, covers the [[main space]] communications bands (S-band and X-band). A [[telemetry]] decoder would be the only needed addition.

Also, the ATA was mentioned as a candidate for searching for a new type of radio [[Transient astronomical event|transient]].<ref>{{cite news | first1=Phil |last1= Berardelli | title=Big Radio from the Stars | url=https://www.science.org/content/article/big-radio-stars | journal=ScienceNOW | date=27 September 2007 | access-date=2009-04-14}}</ref> It is an excellent choice for this owing to its large field of view and wide instantaneous bandwidth. Following this suggestion, [[Andrew Siemion]] and an international team of astronomers and engineers developed an instrument called "Fly's Eye" that allowed the ATA to search for bright radio transients, and observations were carried out between February and April 2008.<ref>{{cite web | title=ATA "Fly's Eye" Pulse Finder | url=http://casper.berkeley.edu/wiki/ATA_%22Fly's_Eye%22_Pulse_Finder | work=Center for Astronomy Signal Processing and Electronics Research (CASPER) | publisher=University of California, Berkeley | date=29 December 2008 | access-date=2009-11-08}}</ref>

== Instruments ==
[[Image:ATA-gregorian.jpg|thumb|The ATA Offset Gregorian Design]]

The ATA-42 configuration will provide a maximum baseline of 300 m (and ultimately for the ATA-350, 900 m). A cooled log-periodic feed on each antenna is designed to provide a system temperature of ~45K from 1–10&nbsp;GHz, with reduced sensitivity in the ranges of 0.5–1.0&nbsp;GHz and 10–11.2&nbsp;GHz. Four separate frequency tunings (IFs) are available to produce 4 x 672&nbsp;MHz intermediate frequency bands. Two IFs support correlators for imaging; two will support [[SETI]] observing. All tunings can produce four dual polarization [[phased array]] beams which can be independently pointed within the primary beam and can be used with a variety of detectors. The ATA can therefore synthesize up to 32 phased array beams.

The wide field of view of the ATA gives it an unparalleled capability for large surveys. The time required for mapping a large area to a given sensitivity is proportional to (''ND'')<sup>2</sup>, where ''N'' is the number of elements and ''D'' is the diameter of the dish. This leads to the surprising result that a large array of small dishes can outperform an array with a smaller number of elements but considerably greater collecting area in the task of large surveys. As a consequence, even the ATA-42 is competitive with much larger telescopes in its capability for both brightness temperature and [[point source]] surveys. For point source surveys, the ATA-42 is comparable in speed to [[Arecibo]] and the [[Green Bank Telescope]] (GBT), but three times slower than the [[Very Large Array]] (VLA). The ATA-350, on the other hand, will be one order of magnitude faster than the Very Large Array for point source surveys, and is comparable to the [[Expanded Very Large Array]] (EVLA) in survey speed. For surveys up to a specified brightness temperature sensitivity, the ATA-98 will exceed the survey speed of even the VLA-D configuration. The ATA-206 should match the brightness temperature sensitivity of [[Arecibo]] and the GBT. The ATA, however, provides better resolution than either of these single-dish telescopes.

The antennas for the ATA are 6.1 x 7.0 meters (20.0&nbsp;ft x 23.0&nbsp;ft) [[hydroforming|hydroformed]] offset [[Gregorian telescope]]s, each with a 2.4 meter sub-reflector with an effective [[focal length]]/diameter (f/D) ratio of 0.65. (See DeBoer, 2001). The offset geometry eliminates blockage, which increases efficiency and decreases the [[side lobe]]s. It also allows for the large sub-reflector, providing good low frequency performance. The hydroforming technology used to make these surfaces is the same as that used by Andersen Manufacturing of Idaho Falls, Idaho to generate low-cost satellite reflectors. The unique interior frame rim-supported compact mount allows excellent performance at low cost. The drive system employs a spring-loaded passive anti-backlash azimuth drive train.  Most components designed by Matthew Fleming and manufactured at Minex Engineering Corp. in [[Antioch, CA]].

==Data management==
As with other [[Astronomical interferometer|arrays]], the huge amount of incoming sensory information requires real-time [[array processing]] capability in order to reduce data volume for storage. For ATA-256, the average data rates and total data volume for the correlator are estimated to be 100 [[Mbyte/s]] and 15 [[Pbyte]]s for the five-year survey period.<ref name="Bower2009">{{Cite web | url=https://usskac.astro.cornell.edu/meetings/USSKAMeetings/USSKA15Oct2009Files/RSSP_RFI2.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100708085226/http://usskac.astro.cornell.edu/meetings/USSKAMeetings/USSKA15Oct2009Files/RSSP_RFI2.pdf | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 8, 2010 |title=A Radio Sky Surveys Project with the Allen Telescope Array - Response to the Request for Information Part 2 |first=Geoffrey C. |last=Bower |date=October 15, 2009}}</ref> Experiments such as [[Transient astronomical event|transient]] surveys will exceed this rate significantly. The [[Beamforming|beamformers]] produce data at a much higher rate (8 [[gigabytes]] per second (Gb/s)) but only a very small fraction of this data is archived. In 2009, the signal detection hardware and software was called Prelude, which was
composed of rack-mounted PCs augmented by two custom accelerator cards based on [[digital signal processing]] (DSP) and [[field-programmable gate array]] (FPGA) chips. Each Programmable Detection Module (one of 28 PCs) can analyze 2&nbsp;MHz of dual-polarization input data to generate spectra with spectral resolution of 0.7&nbsp;Hz and time samples of 1.4 seconds.<ref name="Bower2009"/>

In 2009, the array had a 40 [[Mbit/s]] internet connection, adequate for remote access and transferring of data products for ATA-256. An upgrade to 40 [[Gbit/s]] was planned, which would enable direct distribution of raw data for offsite computing.<ref name="Bower2009"/>

===Computational complexity and requirement===
Like other array systems the ATA has a computational complexity and cross-connect which scales as [[Big O notation|O]](N<sup>2</sup>) with the number of antennas <math>N</math>.
The computation requirement, for example, for correlating the full ATA bandwidth (<math>B</math> = 11&nbsp;GHz) for the proposed <math>N</math> = 350 dual-polarization antenna build-out, using an efficient frequency-multiply [[Array processing#Correlation spectrometer|(FX)]] architecture and a modest 500&nbsp;kHz channel width (with number of channels <math>F</math> = 2200), is given by:<ref>
{{cite book
 | author = Aaron Parsons
 | title = 2006 Fortieth Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems and Computers 
 | date = October 29, 2006 
 | chapter = PetaOp/Second FPGA Signal Processing for SETI and Radio Astronomy  <!-- | journal = Signals, Systems and Computers -->
 | doi = 10.1109/ACSSC.2006.355123
 | pages = 2031–2035 |display-authors=etal| isbn = 978-1-4244-0784-2 
 | s2cid = 10455264 
 }}</ref>

<math>2B \langle N \log_2(F)(10 OPs)+(N \frac{N +1}{2})\times 4(8 OPs) \rangle</math> = 44 [[Peta-]][[Operations per second|OP]]s per second

where <math>Ops</math> is an [[Operation (mathematics)|operation]]. Note that since each dish has a dual polarization antenna, each signal sample is actually a two data set, hence <math>2B</math>.
